ideas.title: The Shariah Rule That Accidentally Optimized for Stablecoins
ideas.trend: Fasset raised $51M Series B in May 2026, becoming the world's first stablecoin-powered Islamic bank with $32B annualized volume across 125 countries including Pakistan, UAE, and Indonesia.
ideas.consensus: Islamic banking is a niche compliance exercise for Muslim-majority markets, constrained by rules that limit its competitiveness against Western fintech.
ideas.angle: The Shariah prohibition on riba (interest) is architecturally aligned with stablecoin payment rails, accidentally building the right infrastructure for the moment stablecoins went mainstream in emerging market payments.

content_pack.x_longform:
The most sophisticated emerging market bank serving Pakistan, Indonesia, and the Gulf might be one that Islamic law prohibits from charging interest.

Fasset raised $51 million this month. Stablecoin-powered, Shariah-compliant, operating across 125 countries, processing $32 billion in annualized volume. The Islamic finance constraint against riba, the taking of interest, turns out to be structurally aligned with stablecoin settlement. Stablecoins move value without a yield component in transit. The prohibition that kept Islamic banks out of consumer lending for decades built the right payment rail before anyone knew payment rails were the product.

The constraint is the product.
x_thread: The most sophisticated emerging market bank serving Pakistan, Indonesia, and the Gulf might be one that Islamic law prohibits from charging interest.
Fasset is a stablecoin-powered Islamic bank. $51M raised this month. Shariah-compliant. Operations in 125 countries. $32 billion in annualized payment volume for more than 1,000 SMBs.

The core constraint: Islamic finance prohibits riba. The taking of interest. The bank can move value but cannot charge for the time value of money. Most Western neobanks are built around the interest-bearing deposit model. Fasset was not.

That constraint turns out to be architecturally aligned with stablecoin settlement. Stablecoins move value from sender to receiver. No interest component in transit. No yield to strip out. The prohibition built the right rail before stablecoins were the obvious choice.

The Islamic finance market is estimated at $3 trillion globally. Most of it runs through banks that layer Shariah compliance on top of Western structures. Fasset built the other direction: native stablecoin rails with Shariah as the foundation.
The constraint is the product.
content_pack.substack_draft:
Most people including myself think of Islamic banking as a compliance exercise. You take a standard banking product, add a Shariah board to sign off on the structure, and call it done. The more I read about Fasset, the more I realized that framing gets the causality completely backwards.

Fasset is a stablecoin-powered Islamic bank. It raised $51 million this month, processes $32 billion in annualized volume across 125 countries, and serves markets that conventional banking either ignores or overcharges. The founding constraint, that Islamic finance prohibits riba, the taking of interest, meant the team could not build around the interest-bearing deposit model that every Western neobank uses. So they built around stablecoin settlement instead. Value moves from sender to receiver without a yield component to strip out or explain away.

What strikes me is that this is not just a compliance workaround. It is structurally simpler. The product does not need to explain APY to a farmer in Islamabad or a remittance sender in Jakarta. It moves dollars cheaply and reliably. That is the entire value proposition.

I am genuinely uncertain whether this scales to a full-service bank or whether it stays a payment infrastructure play. But the constraint that looked like a limitation built exactly the right foundation for the moment stablecoins went mainstream in emerging market payments.

ideas.title: OpenAI Built a Consulting Firm. Its First Investors Are McKinsey and Bain.
ideas.trend: OpenAI launched DeployCo on May 11 2026, a $4B majority-owned subsidiary embedding Forward Deployed Engineers inside enterprise clients, with McKinsey, Bain Capital, and Goldman Sachs among its investors.
ideas.consensus: OpenAI is disrupting knowledge work; consulting firms like McKinsey and Accenture are distribution partners helping enterprises adopt AI.
ideas.angle: The same consulting firms DeployCo is positioned to displace are its founding investors. They funded both sides of the trade before the launch, which is the most sophisticated hedge available when the disruption is happening regardless.

content_pack.x_longform:
OpenAI spent years positioning itself as the company that would make knowledge work obsolete. This month it launched a consulting subsidiary. The investors include McKinsey and Bain Capital.

The entity is called DeployCo. A majority-owned subsidiary backed by $4 billion, launched May 11, designed to embed Forward Deployed Engineers inside enterprise clients and rebuild workflows around AI models. Per eWeek's reporting on the launch, the initial investor list includes McKinsey, Bain Capital, Goldman Sachs, and TPG among 15 other firms. Those are the exact kind of organizations a company automating knowledge work is supposed to be replacing.

The explanation is structural. McKinsey knows that the advice layer requires trust and C-suite relationships a language model cannot build in a single conversation. The bet is that DeployCo owns the technical integration and consulting firms keep the strategic relationship. The FDE embeds the model. The partner pitches the next engagement.

Running alongside is the Frontier Alliance program. Launched in February, per TechCrunch's coverage, it brought Accenture, Capgemini, BCG, and McKinsey into the distribution network for OpenAI's enterprise agent platform. BCG and McKinsey handle strategy. Accenture and Capgemini do systems integration.

So the structure is this. OpenAI has consulting firms distributing its platform. OpenAI's own subsidiary is learning to do what consulting firms do. Both structures coexist by design, per the May 11 announcement. The FDE handles technical implementation. The consultant handles organizational change management.

That coexistence holds as long as the FDE stays in the technical lane. It gets complicated when the FDE, after six months embedded inside an organization, starts getting pulled into the strategy meeting McKinsey used to own.

The consulting firms already modeled that scenario. McKinsey and Bain invested in DeployCo before it launched. They funded the vehicle that is supposed to replace them and secured a seat in the room when it does. That is not a contradiction. That is the most sophisticated hedge available when the disruption is going to happen regardless of whether you fund it.

content_pack.substack_draft:
The consulting industry is roughly 50 years into its current form, and the standard joke has always been that consultants arrive after the crisis, charge for the diagnosis, and leave before implementation fails. OpenAI launched DeployCo this month, a $4 billion subsidiary whose explicit job is to embed engineers inside enterprise clients and rebuild workflows around AI. McKinsey and Bain invested in it. The same firms DeployCo is designed to displace.

I have been trying to figure out whether this is a capitulation or a hedge. McKinsey knows that the billable hour on strategy decks is under pressure. It also knows that C-suite relationships take years to build and a Forward Deployed Engineer cannot develop them in a six-month engagement. So they funded the technical arm and kept the relationship layer for themselves.

The bet works if the FDE and the consultant stay in their respective lanes. It starts to break down if the FDE, after six months embedded inside an organization, begins getting pulled into the meetings McKinsey used to own exclusively. I am not yet sure which way the incentive structure pushes over a three-to-five-year engagement, but the dynamic seems inevitable.

What I keep returning to is that the consulting firms saw this clearly enough to fund it before it launched. That is either the most sophisticated hedge I have watched in professional services or the beginning of a very slow and very polite merger.

ideas.title: The Company Spending 4x Less Just Became the AI Revenue Leader
ideas.trend: Anthropic hit $45B ARR in May 2026, surpassing OpenAI's $33B while projecting 4x lower training spend by 2030; OpenAI projects $14B in losses for 2026 with breakeven pushed to 2030.
ideas.consensus: OpenAI is the AI market leader by brand, ChatGPT usage, and public mindshare.
ideas.angle: Enterprise and consumer AI are structurally different businesses with different unit economics. Anthropic built the enterprise version (80% of revenue) while OpenAI built the famous version. The enterprise version just won the revenue race, and the historical pattern suggests it takes the category.

content_pack.x_longform:
Enterprise and consumer AI are two separate businesses. This month, for the first time, the enterprise version crossed the consumer version in revenue.

Anthropic hit $45 billion in annualized revenue. OpenAI sits at $33 billion. Twelve months ago Anthropic was at $1 billion.

Run the trajectory. $87 million annualized in January 2024. $1 billion by December 2024. $9 billion by end of 2025. $14 billion in February. $19 billion in March. $30 billion in April. $45 billion now. SaaStr's reporting on this describes it as 80x growth in 18 months. No standard model of SaaS growth had a slot for that number.

The training cost comparison adds the structural layer. OpenAI is projected to spend $125 billion annually on model training by 2030. Anthropic's equivalent projection sits around $30 billion. The company spending four times less is generating more revenue. That sentence is worth sitting with.

The cause is in the customer mix. Anthropic runs approximately 80 percent of revenue through enterprise contracts. Business buyers pay per API call on production workflows. KYC pipelines running continuously. Trade reconciliation systems checking millions of transactions daily. Compliance document processing on 60-page policy documents. Fraud screening on every transaction. The compute billed per output token on a live enterprise workflow is structurally different from compute amortized across tens of millions of consumer subscriptions at $20 a month.

Enterprise buyers pay for reliability on the specific workflow. Goldman Sachs deployed Claude for trade reconciliation and client vetting this year. Per CNBC's reporting, client onboarding dropped 30 percent in internal tests. Thousands of manual labor hours saved weekly. The procurement question was whether the model could follow a 60-page compliance policy document reliably through page 40 without inventing something.

OpenAI's answer to the enterprise gap is DeployCo, a $4 billion subsidiary launched this month, embedding Forward Deployed Engineers directly inside enterprise operations to rebuild workflows around AI models. McKinsey, Bain Capital, and Goldman Sachs are among the investors. The same firms DeployCo is positioned to displace funded it before it launched.

The financial trajectories from here diverge badly. OpenAI projects $14 billion in losses in 2026. Anthropic targets positive free cash flow by 2027. OpenAI's own stated breakeven moved to 2030. Both companies spend aggressively on compute. Both declare the same AGI mission. The difference is whether the business that pays for the spending already exists.

ChatGPT has 500 million weekly active users. An extraordinary distribution asset. The question is whether those users convert to enterprise contracts at a rate that closes the revenue gap. Conversion requires compliance certifications, SLA guarantees, and trust built across procurement cycles that take months. Anthropic built those before it built the viral moment. OpenAI built the viral moment first. The enterprise conversion is the harder second act.

IBM embedded itself in corporate payroll and accounting before anyone questioned the value of the hardware lease. Microsoft sold shrinkwrap software while IBM sold the infrastructure contract. Amazon built the logistics cloud while Google printed AdWords revenue. The pattern is consistent: the company that buries itself in enterprise cash flows before the market crowns a winner takes the category.

Anthropic's $45 billion is in enterprise cash flows.

OpenAI's brand is what everyone names when someone asks who is winning AI.

content_pack.substack_draft:
Most people treat the Anthropic vs OpenAI story as a new problem. I do not think it is. It is the same pattern that played out between Amazon and Google in cloud computing, and between Microsoft and IBM before that. The company that builds the unglamorous infrastructure layer quietly wins while the market watches the brand with the better demo.

Anthropic crossed $45 billion in annualized revenue this month. OpenAI is at $33 billion. A year ago Anthropic was at $1 billion. The number that struck me most is the training cost comparison: OpenAI is projected to spend $125 billion a year on model training by 2030. Anthropic's number is around $30 billion. The cheaper model house is generating more revenue.

The reason is the customer mix. Anthropic built enterprise first. Enterprise buyers pay per API call on production workflows: compliance checks, trade reconciliation, client onboarding pipelines running 24 hours a day. Consumer buyers pay $20 a month. The economics are not comparable.

The question I cannot fully answer is whether OpenAI's 500 million weekly active users become the enterprise pipeline or a ceiling. The consumer base is an extraordinary distribution asset. Whether it converts to enterprise cash flows at a rate that closes the gap, I am genuinely not sure. But right now the gap is moving in the wrong direction for OpenAI, and the trajectory that produced $45 billion from $87 million in 18 months does not suggest it is about to slow.
